sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the verse "He set an end to darkness" refers to a limit on the darkness of exile, but unlike other limited things, after this end darkness will no longer be relevant at all.

translations.translation: "He set an end to darkness,"
and it is brought in the Midrash,
"He gave a set time to the world, how many years it will be in darkness."
And the Tzemach Tzedek explains
that it is in the manner of what is said in the Zohar
on the verse,
"To everything there is a season, and a time to every purpose,"
that there is a set time for the darkness of exile.
And it needs to be understood,
since all things in the world have a set time,
"to everything there is a season,"
what is the novelty in "He set an end to darkness"?
And even more so it is not understood,
for from the language of the verse "He set an end to darkness" it implies,
that darkness in and of itself has no end,
rather that He set for it an end.
And one can say the explanation of this,
that this—that undesirable things do not exist during the times that are set aside for good—
is only that they will not then exist in actuality,
for through the good things that exist then,
the undesirable things are nullified.
For it is similar with light and darkness,
that light pushes away darkness
[to the extent that even a little light pushes away a great deal of darkness].
And the concept of "He set an end to darkness" is,
that after its end will come, the concept of darkness will not be relevant at all.
For this—that the future redemption will be an eternal redemption after which there is no exile—
is,
that then the darkness of exile will not be relevant.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the difference between darkness being merely pushed aside or completely nullified depends on the level of light, with limited light only pushing it away and unlimited light eliminating it entirely.

translations.translation: Now, the distinction in the manner of the nullification of darkness—whether it is merely pushed aside by the light,
or its existence is not relevant at all—depends on the level of the light.
For in order to push away darkness
(but even after it is pushed aside, its existence is still relevant)
this is also through a limited light,
to the extent that even a little light pushes away a great deal of darkness.
And in order for the darkness to be completely nullified, it is through an unlimited light.
And as it is brought in the Midrash,
that this—that the redemption of the Exodus from Egypt
(and likewise the redemption from the Babylonian exile and the other exiles, up to the future redemption)
was a redemption after which there was exile,
and the future redemption will be an eternal redemption after which there is no exile,
is,
because the redemption of the Exodus from Egypt is analogous to the light of a candle, which is subject to extinguishing,
and the future redemption is analogous to the light of day, which is not subject to extinguishing.
That is,
the revelation of the future redemption will be a revelation of unlimited light that is not subject to cessation,
and therefore it will be an eternal redemption after which there is no exile.
